name: Cashinahua
confidence_why: Kensinger 1963 describes Peruvian Cashinahua as a two-tone language whose length-marked prominence falls on the first syllable of a stem at phrase level, Capistrano de Abreu 1914 gives fixed final stress for the Brazilian variety, and Oisel et al. 2024 report that Peruvian words differ lexically in stress position (awá 'tapir' but yáwa 'peccary'), so the three first-hand descriptions disagree on both the type and the place of prominence and no word-stress rule can be stated.

catalog_locator: Kensinger 1963: p. 211 sec. 5 'Tonemes', p. 214 secs. 7 'Phonological phrase' and 8 'Phonological clause', p. 215 fn. 4; Capistrano de Abreu 1914: p. 13, p. 29; Oisel et al. 2024: p. 380 fn. 17; Montag 1981: 'Alfabeto cashinahua' page (Rosetta)
catalog_quote: There are two tonemes: high tone and low tone, which though contrastive carry a low semantic load. Only a few grammatical stems contrast with reference to pitch alone, and then only in certain frames, the semantic context indicating which stem is being used. máwáxùkí 'he died', máwáxúkí 'he mimicked something' [...] Analysis of tone perturbations has not been completed. (Kensinger 1963: 211) [...] The nucleus of the phonological phrase is identified by the length of the vowel of the syllable or of the consonant following the vowel, or of both. The nucleus of a phrase is always the first syllable of a grammatical stem. The length of this syllable varies; longer length is accompanied by a tendency for the pitch to glide. [...] The phonological clause consists of one or more phonological phrases. It is characterized by an onset of indrawn breath, a peak of accent on the nucleus of one of the first two phonological phrases, and heavy exhaling or breathiness at closure. (Kensinger 1963: 214) || O accento tonico recai sempre na ultima vogal, excepto si ha ditongo, que vae accentuado na primeira letra. Nas linguas panas do Madeira e do Ucayale o accento tonico prefere a penultima syllaba; mesmo no Juruá ao lado de ka-xi-nau-á ouve-se ka-xi-náu-a.

The nucleus of a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kensinger treats Cashinahua as a two-tone language (high vs. low, low functional load) and does not state a word-stress rule; the closest equivalent is that the prominent (length-marked) nucleus of each phonological phrase is always the first syllable of a grammatical stem, i.e. stem-initial prominence, with a clause-level accent peak on one of the first two phrase nuclei. Older and later sources disagree: Capistrano de Abreu 1914 (Brazilian Caxinauá of the Ibuaçu, p. 13) gives fixed final stress ('O accento tónico recai sempre na ultima vogal, excepto si ha ditongo'), and Oisel et al. 2024 (fn. 17, Peru) treat stress as lexically variable (words ending in a stressed vowel vs. yawa with initial stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Kensinger: each successive phrase nucleus in a clause is progressively shorter than the one bearing clause accent (p. 211).
new_statements.exceptions: Kensinger: tone perturbations not analysed; borders of phrases 'often fuzzy'. Abreu 1914: diphthongs take the accent on their first element; notes variation ka-xi-nau-á ~ ka-xi-náu-a and penultimate accent in Madeira/Ucayali Pano languages. Oisel et al. 2024: stress position differs lexically (final vs. initial) and conditions genitive allomorphy.
new_statements.domain_note: Kensinger's units are phonological phrase and clause, not the word; the stem-initial prominence statement is about phrase nuclei (grammatical stem = word-level unit). Abreu's statement is word-level (citation forms elicited from two speakers). Varieties: Kensinger = Curanja River, Peru (with an Embira, Brazil speaker); Abreu = Ibuaçu/Muru (Tarauacá), Brazil; both are cash1254 per Fleck 2013's index.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources are cash1254 [cbs]. Kensinger 1963 describes the Peruvian Curanja River Cashinahua (with an Embira/Brazil speaker showing no differences); Capistrano de Abreu 1914 describes the Brazilian Caxinauá of the Rio Ibuaçu/Muru (Tarauacá), which Fleck 2013's index equates with Cashinahua [cbs] (distinct from the extinct 'Kashinawa of the Tarauacá River', Glottolog NOCODE); Kaxinawá 2014 and Oisel et al. 2024 describe the Brazilian (Acre) and Peruvian varieties respectively.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress placement rule. The alphabet note presupposes a stressed/unstressed distinction (d > n in unstressed non-initial syllables) but gives no rule for where stress falls. Nothing on tone or vowel length; the Tomo II grammatical appendix excerpt (Rosetta) has no stress or accent term; the sil.org open_url (show_work.asp?id=563) is HTTP 404, so the archive.org copy was used.

Carapanã) and both note that Camargo's data are mainly Peruvian Hãtxa kuĩ (2011 p. 71; 2014 p. 150-151). Montag 1981 and the unreached Montag 1979 / Cromack 1968 describe Peruvian Cashinahua (SIL Peru, Curanja/Purús). Kensinger 1963 (the catalog's existing statement) is also Peruvian. tone.quote: En kaxinawa, las consonantes /n, s, ʂ/ son las únicas que pueden ser codas. El acento tiene como correlato principal la altura tonal; puede conllevar una mayor duración en contextos emotivos. El acento recae en la sílaba final excepto en las formas verbales progresivas … (Camargo 1991: 174-179; cf. Kensinger 1963). … Los datos reportados por Camargo sugieren que el kaxinawa es una lengua yámbica, con la posible excepción de las formas verbales progresivas.
tone.translation: In Kaxinawa, the consonants /n, s, ʂ/ are the only ones that can be codas. Stress has pitch height as its main correlate; it may involve greater duration in emotive contexts. Stress falls on the final syllable except in progressive verb forms … (Camargo 1991: 174-179; cf. Kensinger 1963). … The data reported by Camargo suggest that Kaxinawa is an iambic language, with the possible exception of progressive verb forms.
tone.summary: Metrical survey: treats Kaxinawa as a final-stress (iambic) language whose stress is realised chiefly by pitch height, after Camargo 1991; lexical tone is not discussed for Kaxinawa.
